📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • According to recent reports, after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

According to recent reports, after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

In a recent development, on paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

In a recent development, this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

According to recent reports, jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

In a recent development, having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really major for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

Recent findings suggest that I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

According to recent reports, and then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

In a recent development, and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a substantial thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making upcoming friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

Industry observers note that no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

Recent findings suggest that and so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

It has been revealed that I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Industry observers note that now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

According to recent reports, I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Significant Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard).

A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.

According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction.

The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission.

In a recent development, “The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, said in a statement. “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.”.

Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground.

Just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission launched with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was uninjured, and secured him in a rescue vest to lift him into the aircraft. The mission was finished by 10:45 A.M., and the hiker was transferred to Significant Bend Regional Medical Center.

Sources indicate that “During a complex hoist operation in rugged, inaccessible terrain, our medevac crew successfully reached and evacuated an injured hiker when no ground rescue option existed, delivering the patient safely to higher medical care,” Lt. Col. Teresa Parrotta, commander of the 29th Combat Aviation Brigade, Maryland Army National Guard, mentioned in a statement.

It has been revealed that sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Major Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city. It’s rugged, isolated, and enormous, spanning 800,000 acres with sheer 1,500-foot limestone cliffs. The National Park Service warns visitors to expect unreliable cell service, sparse infrastructure, and primitive roads—conditions compounded by the intense Chihuahuan Desert sandwiched between the Chisos Mountains. Reaching a hiking trailhead is challenging because roads frequently wash out from flash flooding, and many backcountry trails require high-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

Industry News: A Climber We Lost: Jun Kyu Kim

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell.
  • Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters.
  • It has been revealed that jun once said that climbing was the thing he lived for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

Recent findings suggest that on August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which promptly became his true passion.

It has been revealed that jun once said that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee says that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

In a recent development, jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly launched Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

Sources indicate that that was Jun—a man with an unbelievably big heart who was always looking for a way to help and who showed up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

In a recent development, climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

Sources indicate that after a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip. Looking for a crazy-affordable pair that will last for years? The Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes ($50-70) are nearly bulletproof, easy to manipulate with gloves on, and provide a full feature set. This year we added the L.L. Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

In a recent development, snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

Sizes: 22, 25 in Weight: Men’s: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4.1 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 3.6 lbs (22 in), 3.9 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: Men’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 220 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 lbs (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Easy-to-engage heel lift + Very secure binding – Pricey.

According to recent reports, the Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s newly introduced binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she stated.

Sizes: 20.5, 22.5, 26.5 in Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5), 3.8 lbs (22.5), 4lbs (26.5) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (22.5 in), 300 lbs (26.5 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Comfortable stride + Tall heel lift – Expensive.

According to recent reports, the Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of new snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

In a recent development, sizes: 25, 30, 36 in. (men’s) 21, 25 (women’s) Weight: 4.9 lbs (25 in), 5.6 lbs (30 in), 6.5 lbs (36 in) Maximum Load: 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 280 lbs (36 in).

Pros and Cons + Great traction on hills + Easy to adjust, glove-friendly binding + Wide range of sizes – Wider decks can be cumbersome.

According to recent reports, L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging swiftly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a significant plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

On a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Sizes: 22, 25 in. Weight: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Good traction on slopes + Easy-to-use binding + Heel lift – Expensive.

Sources indicate that many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too big for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

Sizes: 20.5, 23.5, 27 in. Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5 in), 3.8 lbs (23.5 in), 4 lbs (27 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (23.5 in), 300 lbs (27 in).

Pros and Cons + Intuitive BOA system + Multi-direction crampons + Flexible + Heel lift – Expensive – No tail extensions – Not great in powder.

Sources indicate that for those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Easy-to-use BOA-style bindings – Below-average traction – No heel lift.

Industry observers note that over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of new snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Sizes: 21, 25, and 30 in. Weight: 4 lbs (21 in), 4.2 lbs (25 in), 4.8 lbs (30 in) Maximum Load: 120-250 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

The double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Pros and Cons + One size fits all + Affordable + Impressive traction + Float tail-compatible – No heel lift.

In a recent development, described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

According to recent reports, the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

The Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of newly introduced snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

In a recent development, the Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

According to recent reports, flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

On the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are crucial for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

Recent findings suggest that in deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or plan to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

According to recent reports, over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

We looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like new bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Kristin Smith A former Backpacker editor, category manager Kristin Smith has been a full- or part-time mountain guide for most of the last decade. Mark your calendar: Outside Days is returning in 2027 with an incredible musical lineup and an inspiring mix of experiences celebrating outdoor culture and community. The fourth annual festival, presented by Capital One and REI Co-op, will take place in Denver, Colorado, at the Auraria Campus in June 2027. It’ll feature three days of music, from June 4 to 6, featuring Jack Johnson, Jungle, Sierra Ferrell, Massive Wild, Trevor Hall, Dr. Dog, and more.

Tickets for Outside Days are on sale Friday, November 20 at 10 A.M. MT.

Sources indicate that music runs three days, June 4 to 6, and features Jack Johnson, Jungle, Sierra Ferrell, Significant Wild, Trevor Hall, Dr. Dog, Almost Monday, Jalen Ngonda, Chance Peña, Medium Build, Amistat, Andy Frasco & The U.N., Steph Strings, Brothers Of Brass, DOGTAGS, The Galentines, and more.

Sources indicate that outside Days is more than a festival you attend; it’s one you join. From live music and inspiring conversations to hands-on experiences that invite exploration and discovery, the festival brings people together around a shared passion for the outdoors.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the music, attendees can explore adventure film screenings, hear from world-renowned athletes, explorers, and storytellers, and take part in activities ranging from climbing and overlanding to wellness, outdoor cooking, and gear demonstrations. Many of these experiences are created in collaboration with Outside’s brand partners, giving festivalgoers new ways to learn, play, and connect.

Also returning is the Outside Days Industry Conference, which precedes the festival on Thursday and Friday, June 3 and 4, and features thought-provoking panels, interactive workshops, and curated networking experiences for professionals across the outdoor, travel, and active lifestyle industries. An Industry Pass includes access to the conference and the festival’s opening night, while bundled passes extend access through the full weekend.

According to recent reports, as the presenting sponsor of Outside Days, Capital One is offering cardholders early access to tickets and exclusive festival perks, including express entry, special discounts, and access to the Capital One Cardholder Lounge. Eligible Capital One Credit and Debit Cardholders, including REI Co-op® Mastercard® holders, can purchase presale tickets starting Monday, November 16 at 10 A.M. MT through Thursday, November 19 at 10 A.M. MT, while supplies last. Tickets must be purchased using an eligible Capital One card during the presale window. Excludes Capital One-issued private label cards. Terms apply.

Tickets go on sale to the general public on Friday, November 20 at 10 A.M. MT, with early bird pricing available while supplies last.

Recent findings suggest that prices are inclusive of fees for general admission. VIP packages feature access to premium main stage viewing and the VIP lounge. New for 2027, the Super VIP (SVIP) ticket offers the ultimate festival experience starting at $324.50 for a single day.

Outside+ members can add access to the Outside+ lounge when purchasing general admission or VIP three-day tickets and receive $25 off the upgrade. Special meet-and-greets with elite athletes and outdoor luminaries will be included with Outside+ lounge access, plus perks like private bathrooms and exclusive food and beverage options. #67756. Latest Update: How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4413 w)

Latest Update: How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

These nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

Industry observers note that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

It has been revealed that complications with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “strategy falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

In a recent development, what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

If pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

In a recent development, the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

Sources indicate that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

An alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

In a recent development, have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

If it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

In a recent development, the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

The most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

According to recent reports, the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

Industry observers note that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

According to recent reports, the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

If the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

Industry observers note that if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

According to recent reports, once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

In a recent development, even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

In a recent development, besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

In a recent development, let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

Recent findings suggest that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done rapidly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a big, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is key.

Lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

If you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

Recent findings suggest that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

While you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a newly introduced stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

Industry observers note that but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is notable. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

According to recent reports, lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

According to recent reports, if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

Sources indicate that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

Speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

According to recent reports, see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Sources indicate that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

It has been revealed that with all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the massive ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

In a recent development, it’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Recent findings suggest that hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Substantial Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Massive Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Sources indicate that crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

Sources indicate that one of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Recent findings suggest that perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Sources indicate that desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

Sources indicate that on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

Industry observers note that my favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

Mt. Joy frontman Matt Quinn has been visiting national parks his whole life. He’s found healing energy in nature and taken inspiration from the magic and fragility of places like the Maine coastline. So when we asked him to play Park Sessions in Acadia National Park, it was a natural fit. His music is in perfect harmony with nature’s stage.

During his visit to Acadia National Park with the Park Sessions crew, Quinn practices the art of slowing down—immersing himself in the Maine landscape, wildlife, and culture. He takes the winding roads around Mount Desert Island in the agile and spacious Mazda CX-50, taking in the scenery as it changes from rocky coast to dense evergreen forest. Amid settings ranging from primitive skills lessons to beekeeping to lobster cookouts on the beach, Quinn’s set in Acadia is more than a performance—it’s a spiritual deep dive into what makes this park special. It’s a connection between music and the places that inspire it.

Take a hike: From the Sand Beach parking area, take the Ocean Path Trail. This 2.2-mile out-and-back trail will take you to some of Acadia’s best-known highlights, including Thunder Hole and Otter Point.

It has been revealed that learn something latest: Primitive skills instructor Mike Douglas taught Quinn how to start fire with a bow drill and how to feel his way through nature. You can hone your own outdoor skills through a variety of programs with the Maine Primitive Skills School.

2026 Mazda CX-50 2.5 S Preferred with options shownOutside.

According to recent reports, go for a scenic drive: The winding Cadillac Summit Road takes you past scenic vistas and through changing scenery as you drive to the summit of Cadillac Mountain. Hike the short loop at the top to get the most of the 360-degree views.

Eat like a Mainer: There’s no shortage of fresh lobster, lobster rolls, and scallops near Acadia National Park. Indulge in the coastal flavors, then learn how the industry works with Emma Fernald, founder of Bay Lady Scallops. The seventh-generation lobsterman offers farm tours and shows folks how to pull in a lobster trap.

Industry observers note that matt Quinn is the co-founder and singer-songwriter behind Mt. Joy, an indie-folk band known for its soaring melodies, thoughtful storytelling, and road-trip-ready anthems. Long before Quinn was performing for large public audiences, it was public land that helped name his band. Mt. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm.
  • Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

There is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

According to recent reports, but can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

It has been revealed that however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

In a recent development, I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a massive-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

Sources indicate that my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

According to recent reports, I watched The Alpinist on the substantial screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Industry observers note that nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

#67751. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2722 w)
