When can a kid ride in the front seat?

📅 03 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moms

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com.
  • In a recent development, she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years.
  • She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

In a recent development, she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

In a recent development, katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite demonstrates for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

It has been revealed that has your major kid started asking – or downright begging – to graduate to the front seat of the car finally? Most kids start pining for the coveted spot long before they are big enough to safely sit up front.

According to recent reports, of course,safetyis your number one concern, butas their endless pleas wear you down, you might be wondering:when can I let them sit up front? Is it really that massive of a deal to keep them in the back? We’ve been there. For help, we reached out to childhood safety experts to understand why the AAP recommends waiting until at least the age of 13 before letting your child ride in the front seat.

It has been revealed that while the AAP guidelines are clear, local and federal laws (or, rather, lack thereof) muddy the waters. Lia Tuso, a Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST) based in Buffalo, New York, tells Moms.com, “Unfortunately, when it comes to child passenger safety, the laws are the bare minimum.” There are no federal laws in the U.S. prohibiting children from riding in the front seat, but there are a handful of state laws. Delaware, for example, requires children to be at least 12 years old and 65 inches tall to sit in the front seat, while California mandates that children must be eight years old and over 57 inches tall. And it’s not just the U.S. – other peer nations’ laws are surprisingly lax around the topic. Most state laws in Australia, for example, require children to be at least seven years old to ride shotgun.

Recent findings suggest that tuso does not mince words about why younger children in the front seat of a car is so dangerous, saying, “The frontal airbags are designed to protect adult male bodies, not pre-pubescent children. The frontal airbags deploy at about 200 mph and they are designed to make contact with the average-sized male adult's bones. They simply aren't designed to protect children who don't have the same bone strength as an adult.”.

Recent findings suggest that corri Miller-Hobbs, a safety expert with the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU, agrees. She also oversees the Virginia chapter Safe Kids Worldwide and tells Moms.com, “[Keeping children under 13 in the back seat] places the child in a seating position that is further away from a frontal crash, the most common type of crash.”.

In a recent development, tuso points out that research performed by the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia shows that children who are exposed to frontal airbags are twice as likely to suffer injury than children riding in the back seat. “The injuries that are most frequently seen from children riding in the front seat are head injuries such as traumatic brain injury and superficial head trauma, thoracic/chest injuries, abdominal injuries, pelvic injuries, and orthopedic injuries such as long bone fractures,” Dr. Alexis Javier, a Pediatrician with Memorial Hermann Health System in Houston, Texas, tells Moms.com. Importantly, Miller-Hobbs adds, “Injuries vary and can depend on how close the child is sitting to the frontal airbag and whether they were correctly restrained with a child restraint or safety belt.”.

Tuso recommends seeking guidance from Child Passenger Safety Technician for every car seat transition, saying that too often, “parents will schedule a car seat installation check with a CPST for their newborn, but don't finish the journey to the front seat.”.

According to recent reports, “Oftentimes we see kids sitting upfront, who should still not only be in the back seat, but also in a booster!” Tuso notes, “Most children will need a booster until ten to 12 years old. So parents should first ask, has the child maxed out the height/weight limits on their current booster seat?”.

In addition to being physically developed enough to be safe in the front seat, Tuso shares crucial guidelines to ensure the correct fit for an adult seatbelt on a child, called the Five-Step Test.

“Even if your child passes the seat belt fit test in one seating position in one vehicle, that doesn’t mean they will pass the test in all vehicles and seating positions… so be sure to perform the seat belt fit test in any vehicle and any seating position your child may utilize,” Miller-Hobbs claims. She also advises moving the passenger seat as far back from the airbag as possible for your child.

“Be sure to consider your child’s developmental level and personality when explaining the rationale,” Miller-Hobbs indicates, “Avoid using scary details about injuries versus talking about making healthy and safe choices, as with other aspects of their life.” She offers a few ideas to help make the backseat more appealing, such as:.

In a recent development, tuso adds that watching crash test videos together on YouTube can be an effective way to demonstrate the necessity for strict rules around riding up front. “There is a lot of peer pressure around this age, especially with school drop-offs, but reminding your child of the importance of riding safely will set them up for success... even when they're driving on their own!” she states.

“We understand caregivers and children are excited and proud when new milestones are achieved,” Miller-Hobbs adds, “However, moving out of a car seat or belt positioning booster seat into a seat belt system should not be a milestone that is rushed.” Tuso agrees, saying, “The safest place for children under 13 is the back seat. While growing up is inevitable, injuries are preventable... there's no rush to the front seat.”.

#67646. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

📅 09 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How should we all tackle phone use and screen time?
  • Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?
  • I don’t see much evidence of it out there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

In a recent development, I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have stated,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”.

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”.

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The Upcoming York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”.

In a recent development, bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”.

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a substantial piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity?
  • It has been revealed that I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Industry observers note that will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

It has been revealed that I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

According to recent reports, “I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he stated to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”.

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he states, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”.

Industry observers note that finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”.

Sources indicate that in 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Industry observers note that danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

According to recent reports, masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

Self-Gifting Ideas For Moms: 28 Holiday Gifts To Treat Yourself

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oh, we’re stuffing our own stockings again?
  • Recent findings suggest that every December, moms pull off a small miracle, and we do it mostly on our own.
  • Recent findings suggest that if your family actually remembers to toss a present or two under the tree or in the stocking for you, you’ve probably grown accustomed to getting the same gift, or some variation of it, every year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oh, we’re stuffing our own stockings again? Well, they’re gonna be filled with things we love, gosh damn it.

Recent findings suggest that every December, moms pull off a small miracle, and we do it mostly on our own. The presents get bought, wrapped, and tucked under the tree with tender care. The stockings get stuffed, the Elf gets Shelf’ed, the fridge and pantry get filled with foods everyone in the family (even your little picky eater) will enjoy. And nearly every December, moms end up with an empty stocking or whatever drugstore special got picked up last-minute because, oops, Mom doesn’t have anything under the tree again!

Recent findings suggest that if your family actually remembers to toss a present or two under the tree or in the stocking for you, you’ve probably grown accustomed to getting the same gift, or some variation of it, every year. A “World’s Best Mom” mug. A bath bomb. You know the type. It’s fine. Really. We know it’s the thought that counts! But we also know that moms spend the entire holiday season thinking about everyone else’s wish lists, and nobody’s thinking very hard about ours.

According to recent reports, that’s exactly why we here at Scary Mommy are big fans of taking matters into our own hands. Buy these gifts for yourself, stuff your own stocking, use ‘em to drop some very unsubtle hints on your partner’s phone, or forward this list straight to your friends and family. Because you, dear friend, deserve gifts you’ll genuinely love... and not another GD bath bomb (unless that’s your thing).

Every time I put these on the bed, my husband and I waller around like piggies in mud. They're so soft! You must waller, smiling with your eyes shut, to really enjoy them. I adore everything about these sheets and am jonesing to replace some of our old cheap sheet sets with more. They feel breathable, don't make my night sweats worse like cheap sheets do, and they actually STAY on our mattress. We all know there's nothing worse than laying on a bunch of wrinkles all night once your fitted sheet pops off a corner. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

It has been revealed that for the woman on your holiday list who is thoughtful about what goes on her skin, this is such a beautiful and meaningful gift. The Golden Beryl Moisturizer is a lightweight, non-greasy daily hydrator packed with organic turmeric root, ginger root, bearberry extract, hyaluronic acid, CoQ10, and Vitamin C, all formulated to brighten, even tone, and support the skin barrier without a harsh ingredient in sight. The entire Golden Beryl Collection is hormone-conscious, Leaping Bunny certified, pregnancy-safe, and free from parabens, phthalates, sulfates, and synthetic fragrances, which in clean beauty is genuinely rare. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

Ever since having my delightful children 10+ years ago, I've been on — shall we say — a hair journey. My hair has done the postpartum fall out, it's done the regrowth, and now, years later, it's graying, changing texture, and, once again, falling out. This stuff is great to help combat that, plus it makes my hair super shiny. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

Industry observers note that if you've been waiting for someone to get you a red light therapy mask, and they just haven't, well, now is your time, girl! I love this one because it's so comfortable and looks so lovely — while delivering 360-degree red light coverage that's FDA-approved. I'm all about beauty finds that are evidence-based, and this fits the ticket. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Everyone who has ever set foot in my house knows I almost always have at least one candle burning. I just think it makes everything feel so cozy and welcoming! And this candle subscription box is the perfect thing to keep me stocked and happy. With the Luxe Box, you get two 16-ounce soy candles every month from different independent American candle makers. I really appreciate the little backstories included, and how they highlight women- and minority-owned makers. The candles smell DIVINE, and they come in super frickin’ cute little printed cloth bags. It’s just such a fun treat to look forward to each month. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

In a recent development, I have been eyeing this Noon & Moon mug for literal years. It's so pretty and cozy and cottagecore, but the price point always had me closing out of the tab without adding to cart. But isn't that the kind of item, the one you usually won't buy yourself but know you'll use and love so often, that makes the perfect gift? — Katie McPherson.

It has been revealed that this palette is on my personal wish list, and I cannot stop thinking about it. Chokehold Cosmetics is an indie brand, and this palette delivers on that with seven highly pigmented eyeshadow shades, from soft matte beige to molten gold shimmer to blood red, plus a warm blush and an unapologetic highlighter, all in one gorgeous compact. It is vegan, cruelty-free, and the shade names alone — Undressed, Shackle, Bite Mark, Blood Oath — tell you exactly the kind of energy this brand is bringing. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that I have tried every single water bottle and tumbler cup on the market, and I mean every.single.one. This one is my favorite. It sips like a straw (but the shape means no mouth wrinkles!), doesn't hurt my sensitive teeth, the straw never falls out and forces me to stick my hands into the water to get it so I can keep drinking...and yes, it keeps my water cold forever. I was worried the snap-shut lid wouldn't be strong enough to stay closed, and maybe if you want to toss your water bottle in a bag and not worry about it at all, it wouldn't. But for someone who carries their water bottle and at most lays it down in the seat of my car, it has prevented spills just fine. And bless, it doesn't spurt water up at you when it's been closed and jostled around a little. That's my pet peeve. — Katie McPherson.

Harry & David’s Moose Munch is the iconic caramel popcorn drizzled with chocolate and loaded with premium mix-ins that has been a cult holiday snack for decades, and for very good reason. It is the kind of treat that sits on the counter and disappears faster than you planned for, and the holiday tins and gift boxes make it feel genuinely special rather than just a bag of snacks. It’s the “buy it for yourself” gift that you absolutely deserve and will not regret for a single second! — Katie Garrity.

I burn candles constantly, and I love finding a fresh candle brand to try out. Paddywax makes some of the cutest candle vessels that you'll want to keep long after the wax runs out. This Smoked Cherry scent is beautiful and elevated, a not-too-cloying way to enjoy a cherry fragrance if you're into them. As soon as I smelled it I wanted five more, and it has a great throw that fills the room. — Katie McPherson.

Sources indicate that this kitchen bundle is the gift-for-yourself upgrade that makes every single meal feel more intentional: 10 solid, one-piece teak utensils covering every cooking task, from spatulas and a ladle to a pasta server, skimmer, and salad fork, plus three bamboo cutting boards in three sizes so there is always the right board for the job. The teak wood is smooth, sturdy, scratch-free on nonstick cookware, and has a warm, beautiful grain that makes the whole kitchen feel pulled together just by sitting out. — Katie Garrity.

I'd never smelled a Fulton & Roark fragrance until this year, and now I'm obsessed with multiple. Calle Ocho is a gourmand lover's dream. Lover's Lane has a gorgeous deep fruity vibe that I keep reaching for in winter, while Hwy 190 was my summer go-to. The Discovery sets are a great way to smell a range of options from the brand, and they come with a $30 coupon code to spend on a full-size perfume once you pick your favorite. In short, they scream "stuff me in a stocking." — Katie McPherson.

It has been revealed that this set has completely elevated my morning skincare routine, and it is the buy-it-for-yourself gift that actually gets used every single day. The Sweet July Morning Essentials Set includes the Pava Exfoliating Cleanser, Pava Toner, Soursop Vitamin C Serum, and Castaway Cream, all inspired by founder Ayesha Curry’s Jamaican heritage and packed with Caribbean superfoods like papaya, guava, and soursop that make your skin look genuinely luminous. Everything is clean, vegan, cruelty-free, and formulated for all skin tones and types, which means it actually works rather than just sitting on a shelf looking pretty. It’s the morning routine upgrade that makes getting out of bed worth it because your skin is going to look that good. — Katie Garrity.

In a recent development, you want to pick out your own skincare anyway, but if you send this to your partner on a wishlist you'll probably have to hear about the price. But if you have extremely dry skin that has never responded well to retinol of any kind, I beg you to put this under the tree for yourself. My skin will not tolerate retinol at all, but this product gives me the healthiest plump and glow without any irritation. I've had numerous people ask me what I'm doing differently with my skin since I started using it (and because it's gentle enough to use multiple nights a week, I actually get results, not just flakes and irritation). — Katie McPherson.

This is genuinely one of my favorite discoveries of the year and absolutely qualifies as a gift to yourself. Delta makes hemp-derived THC sparkling beverages in the most delicious flavors that deliver a light, relaxing buzz without the next-morning regret that comes with alcohol. Each can has a precise, low dose so you always know exactly what you are getting; the effect is that perfect mellow, calm feeling that makes a Tuesday night on the couch feel like a genuine treat, and they taste like something a fancy cocktail bar would charge way too much for. — Katie Garrity.

Jasmine Dowling Plum Polka Dot Phone Case.

Look, I get not wanting to spend a ton of money on a phone case, but recently I realized how much I use them and how much better a good one protects my very expensive little pocket computer. The Dairy's are so pretty and on trend, and I love all the matching accessories. They're tough too. I snagged a MagSafe case so I can use a magnetic grip on the back (helps my wrists), as well as the matching battery pack for when I'm out and about and suddenly realize I'm at 10%. Also, I love that they commission designs from real artists for their cases (this one is by Jasmine Dowling). — Katie McPherson.

These notecards are one of those purchases that make you feel like a more elevated version of yourself. The Liberty London floral prints are absolutely stunning, the paper quality is thick and luxurious, and there is something genuinely joyful about having a set of notecards this beautiful sitting on your desk ready to go. Sending a handwritten note feels like a lost art, and this set makes you want to bring it back immediately, whether it is a thank you, a thinking of you, or just an excuse to use something this pretty. — Katie Garrity.

I’ve been wanting to try Prose custom hair and skincare for so long; the holidays feel like the perfect time to treat myself! I am loving using shampoo, conditioner, and skincare formulated specifically for my needs, goals, and routine. You just take their quick (but thorough) online consultation and, voila, Prose whips up stuff just for you. They even put your name on the bottles! I think this would make such a thoughtful gift for another mom, or even for a teen. We got my 15-year-old a set, and they’re just as hooked as I am. — Julie Sprankles.

This sweatshirt is the buy-it-for-yourself purchase that requires absolutely zero justification. It is cozy, it is Winnie the Pooh, and it makes every single person who sees you wearing it immediately smile, which is honestly a public service. The fit is relaxed and comfortable without being shapeless, the graphic is that perfect nostalgic Disney art style that hits every millennial who grew up watching the Hundred Acre Wood, and it is the kind of piece you reach for on every cozy fall and winter morning without thinking twice. Permission granted to add to cart immediately! — Katie Garrity.

For the woman who takes her candles seriously, this is the one worth buying for yourself this season. The Amélie is a warm, complex, deeply luxurious blend of saffron and oud that fills a room without being overwhelming, and it has that rich, sophisticated scent profile that makes your home smell like a boutique hotel rather than a Yankee Candle. La Jolie Muse uses natural soy wax, cotton wicks, and fragrance oils that actually throw scent properly rather than disappearing after twenty minutes. — Katie Garrity.

Over the years, my makeup routine has become much more streamlined. I don’t have time for a 12-step routine, but I do have time for two steps that make me look and feel way more put-together than I actually am most days. And this Iconic Londo duo happens to come with both of those products, which, for the record, are consistent refills for me. The Underglow Blurring Primer is hands-down my go-to primer; it smooths over my pores, makes my makeup glide on beautifully, and gives me that dreamy soft-focus finish. Then I finish with the cult-favorite Prep-Set-Glow mist, which leaves my skin dewy and radiant. — Julie Sprankles.

I love having high-quality, soft-as-heck blankets all over my house. I think it's one of the main things that makes people tell me how cozy my home is. When I want to buy myself a nice gift, I cannot go wrong buying a lovely throw, and this one by Tourance truly feels as soft as a rabbit, but without doing any harm to animals. It is worth the price! — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that these glasses are one of my favorite things I own, and they make every drink feel like an occasion. The Lotus Coupe has the most beautiful, organic petal-shaped silhouette that looks genuinely sculptural sitting on a shelf or a bar cart, and the hand-blown quality means each one is slightly unique in the most intentional, artisan way. Whether you are pouring a proper cocktail, a glass of sparkling wine, or honestly just sparkling water because you deserve fancy glassware regardless, these elevate the whole experience. — Katie Garrity.

Bogg bags have been having a serious moment for a while now, and the Go Tote is the version that makes the most sense for everyday life. It is a 20L structured tote with that signature washable EVA material that wipes clean instantly, holds its shape no matter what you put in it, and has an interior that actually fits everything without becoming a bottomless pit you have to dig through. The Café Au Lait colorway is a warm, neutral latte tone that goes with absolutely everything and works year-round without feeling too summery or too seasonal. — Katie Garrity.

I have always, always been a sucker for gourmand scents, and this one is what I would call a grown-up gourmand. Not cloying, not overpowering, just a dreamy whipped and fluffy body cream that begs to be slathered all over. With its key notes of strawberry, pink marshmallow, and whipped vanilla, it smells like a fancy dessert, which is a treat in and of itself. But thanks to a blend of hyaluronic acid and rich oils, it’s super hydrating and leaves my skin extra soft. Great for layering! — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that this is the hair product that quietly became a cult favorite for very good reason. Lush Super Milk is a leave-in conditioning primer that you spray on damp hair before styling to protect against heat, reduce frizz, add shine, and genuinely improve your hair’s texture over time with consistent use. It is lightweight enough that it does not weigh hair down or leave any residue, it smells absolutely incredible, and it is the kind of step you add to your routine once and then can never imagine skipping again. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that this vacuum has completely changed my relationship with keeping the floors clean, and it is absolutely a buy-it-for-yourself moment. The cordless design means I actually vacuum more because there is zero friction in grabbing it and going (rather than hunting for an outlet and wrestling with a cord), and the suction power is genuinely impressive for something this lightweight and maneuverable. It handles hardwood, rugs, and everything in between without missing a beat, and the fact that it converts to a handheld means I can get to the couch cushions, the stairs, and the car without swapping to a different tool. — Katie Garrity.
